questions.q: What is the CTA review board, structurally?
options: A multiple-choice exam taken online with no human panel
A panel exam where a candidate presents a proposed architecture for a given scenario, then defends it under extended Q&A from CTA-certified judges
An automated score generated from a candidate's Trailhead badge count
A peer-reviewed code submission with no live presentation component
questions.explain: The review board is an interactive panel exam: present a design for a given scenario, then field challenging follow-up questions from judges.

questions.q: Which named prerequisite certification domain does this entire course correspond to?
options: Sharing and Visibility Designer
Integration Architecture Designer
Identity and Access Management Designer
Development Lifecycle and Deployment Designer
questions.explain: Sharing and Visibility Designer is one of the individually-certifiable prerequisite domains candidates must hold before sitting the CTA review board.

questions.q: How does the review board's scoring philosophy treat a candidate who openly explains a design trade-off versus one who rigidly defends an original answer after a flaw is pointed out?
options: Open trade-off explanation and adaptability are generally viewed more favorably than defending a flawed design unchanged
Both are scored identically, since only the final design matters
Rigid defense of an unchanged answer is generally scored higher, since it signals confidence
The board does not evaluate reasoning at all, only whether the design technically functions
questions.explain: The board is widely described as rubric-based and trade-off-aware — sound, adaptable reasoning tends to score better than stubbornly defending an original design once a real flaw surfaces.

questions.q: In the mock scenario, why was a criteria-based sharing rule (not an owner-based mechanism) used to grant the compliance team visibility into hazmat Opportunities?
options: Criteria-based rules are always cheaper to build than any other sharing mechanism
Criteria-based rules re-evaluate on the flagged field rather than the owner, so visibility survives the Opportunity being reassigned to a different owner
Owner-based sharing rules do not exist in Salesforce
The compliance team needed write access, which only criteria-based rules can grant
questions.explain: Because the rule's criteria is the Hazmat Contract field, not the owner, reassigning the deal to a different account executive doesn't affect the compliance group's access — exactly the durability the requirement needed.

questions.q: Why did the mock design use role hierarchy (hub-based roles) for dispatch-manager visibility instead of just setting Opportunity OWD to Public Read Only?
options: Public Read Only is not a valid OWD setting for Opportunity
Role hierarchy is always faster to configure than any OWD change
Public Read Only would expose every hub's deals to every account executive org-wide, which the requirement never asked for and unnecessarily widens exposure of sensitive data
OWD settings cannot coexist with sharing rules in the same org
questions.explain: The requirement only asked for each hub's dispatch manager to see their own hub — a role-hierarchy grant under Private OWD satisfies that without the unjustified org-wide exposure a looser OWD setting would create.
